summary: For strix, the most robust path to validated actions from a local model in Go is to NOT rely on the model "behaving" — instead use grammar-constrained decoding so output is guaranteed structurally valid, then validate semantically in Go, then gate through the deterministic Scope Guard. The recommended stack is: the official Ollama Go client (github.com/ollama/ollama/api) as the LLM transport, using its ChatRequest.Format (json.RawMessage holding a JSON Schema) to force structured output — Ollama compiles that schema to a GBNF grammar in llama.cpp and masks invalid tokens at sample time, so malformed JSON is impossible at the token level. Native Ollama tool-calling (ChatRequest.Tools + resp.Message.ToolCalls) is mature as of 2025 (new structure-aware streaming parser, May 2025) and gives you OpenAI-style tool calls, but arguments are NOT schema-validated, only parsed — so a validate-and-repair layer is mandatory. Layer santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6 (validation, draft 2020-12) over the decoded args, with invopop/jsonschema or Google's new google/jsonschema-go (Jan 2026) to generate the schemas from Go structs. Wrap it all in a small validate->repair->retry loop (1-2 retries, temp 0, re-prompt with the validation error) before handing the action to the Scope Guard. Avoid langchaingo as the core abstraction — it works but adds a heavy dependency, lags the raw client, and you give up fine control you need for an auditable security tool. For maximum determinism (or non-Ollama deployments) you can shell to llama.cpp's server and use its json_schema/grammar fields directly. Model-wise, Qwen3 (14B/32B), Llama 3.1/3.3, and Devstral are the well-supported tool-callers; force-constrain output regardless of model.

recommendations.name: Ollama Go client + Format=JSON Schema (github.com/ollama/ollama/api)
recommendations.why: This is the spine of the recommended approach. The official Go client is a first-party, single-import package that maps 1:1 to the local Ollama HTTP API. Set ChatRequest.Format (typed json.RawMessage) to a JSON Schema and Ollama compiles it to a GBNF grammar inside llama.cpp; invalid tokens are masked during sampling, so resp.Message.Content is GUARANTEED to be structurally-valid JSON matching the schema — you json.Unmarshal it directly. This eliminates the entire class of 'model emitted broken JSON' failures, which is exactly what an auditable pen-test tool needs. Tradeoff: schema-constraint guarantees structure/types, not semantic correctness (e.g. an in-scope IP), so you still validate in Go and gate through Scope Guard. Keep schemas shallow — deeply nested/recursive schemas degrade quality and speed.
recommendations.integration: go-lib (import github.com/ollama/ollama/api; client = api.ClientFromEnvironment(); client.Chat(ctx, &api.ChatRequest{Model, Messages, Format: schemaJSON}, handler)). Requires a local ollama daemon (also MIT, runs offline, no key).
recommendations.language: Go (client); Ollama server is Go wrapping llama.cpp (C++)
recommendations.maturity: Mature and first-party; tracks the server release-for-release. ChatRequest exposes Format, Tools, Options, Think, Logprobs as of 2025-2026.

recommendations.name: Native Ollama tool calling (ChatRequest.Tools / resp.Message.ToolCalls)
recommendations.why: Use this when you want the model to CHOOSE among strix's registered tools (portscan, etc.) rather than just fill one fixed schema. Define api.Tool{Type:"function", Function: api.ToolFunction{Name, Description, Parameters}} per registered plugin; the model returns resp.Message.ToolCalls[].Function.{Name, Arguments}. As of the May 2025 streaming-tool release, Ollama's parser is structure-aware (reads each model's template, streams tool calls, dedupes) — much more reliable than the old JSON-sniffing parser. Tradeoff vs. Format: tool-call Arguments are parsed but NOT grammar-constrained or schema-validated, so the validate-and-repair layer is REQUIRED here. Works on Qwen3, Llama 3.1/3.3/4, Devstral, Qwen2.5; needs >=32k context for good multi-tool behavior. Recommended hybrid for strix: use Tools for tool SELECTION, then a Format-constrained second call (or per-tool grammar) to fill that tool's arguments.
recommendations.integration: go-lib (same api package). Map your tool registry -> api.Tools; dispatch on ToolCalls[].Function.Name; feed results back as api.Message{Role:"tool"}.
recommendations.maturity: Mature for mainstream tool-trained models; accuracy still varies by model size — larger models needed for multi-tool/multi-step. Arguments unvalidated by design.

recommendations.name: santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6 (validation) + invopop/jsonschema or google/jsonschema-go (schema generation)
recommendations.why: The validate half of validate-and-repair. santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6 is the de-facto Go JSON Schema validator (drafts 4 through 2020-12), pure-Go, no cgo, gives precise per-field errors you can feed back into a repair prompt. It does NOT generate schemas, so pair it with a generator: invopop/jsonschema (mature, draft 2020-12, reflects Go structs via tags) or Google's new google/jsonschema-go/jsonschema (released Jan 2026, official, reflects structs and represents the spec as a plain Go struct — also what the Go MCP SDK uses). Generate schema from your action/arg structs once, send it as Ollama's Format AND validate decoded output against it — single source of truth. This is what turns untrusted model text into typed actions safe to pass to Scope Guard.
recommendations.license: santhosh-tekuri: Apache-2.0; invopop: MIT; google/jsonschema-go: BSD-3-Clause
recommendations.integration: go-lib (all three). Reflect struct -> schema (invopop/google) -> marshal as Format -> on response Unmarshal -> Validate (santhosh-tekuri) -> on error, repair-retry.
recommendations.maturity: santhosh-tekuri and invopop are widely used and stable; google/jsonschema-go is new (2026) but official and tied to the Go MCP SDK — safe to adopt, lighter spec coverage than santhosh for validation so keep santhosh for the validator role.

recommendations.name: Validate->repair->retry loop (hand-rolled in Go, ~50 lines)
recommendations.why: The reliability glue, and small enough to own rather than pull a framework. Pattern: (1) request with Format=schema and temperature 0 (or low), (2) json.Unmarshal, (3) jsonschema.Validate, (4) on parse/validate failure, append the exact error text as a user/tool message ('your output failed: <err>, return corrected JSON only') and retry, capped at 1-2 attempts, (5) on repeated failure, FAIL CLOSED — emit an audited error, never execute an unvalidated action. Because you also use Format-constrained decoding, step 2/3 should rarely trip, so retries stay near zero. Owning this loop (vs. instructor/langchaingo) keeps strix a single static binary, keeps every attempt in the audit log, and lets the Scope Guard remain the final non-AI gate. Monitor format-failure-rate (<1%) and avg-retry (<1.5) as health metrics.
recommendations.integration: Native Go in strix's plan->guard->execute engine, sitting between planner output and Scope Guard.
recommendations.maturity: Pattern is industry-standard (Instructor/LangChain replicate it); trivial and robust to implement incrementally.

recommendations.name: llama.cpp server json_schema/grammar (fallback / max-determinism path)
recommendations.why: Alternative to Ollama for operators who want to drive the inference engine directly or run fully air-gapped without the Ollama daemon. llama.cpp's server (and llama-cli) accept a json_schema field OR a raw GBNF grammar on /completion and /v1/chat/completions; it converts schema->GBNF (json_schema_to_grammar) and masks tokens, same guarantee as Ollama (Ollama is a wrapper over this). Lets you author a hand-tuned GBNF grammar when a JSON Schema can't express a constraint (e.g. a tight enum/regex for a tool name). Tradeoff: you manage the server binary/model files and HTTP plumbing yourself; less convenient than Ollama for the default UX. Keep Ollama as default, document this as the power-user/air-gapped backend behind the same Go interface.
recommendations.integration: shell-out CLI (spawn llama-server) + HTTP from Go (POST json_schema or grammar to /v1/chat/completions). No Go bindings needed; treat as an interchangeable backend behind strix's LLM interface.
recommendations.language: C++ (server); strix talks to it over HTTP from Go
recommendations.maturity: Very mature, actively maintained (ggml-org); grammar-constrained decoding is a core, battle-tested feature.

pitfalls: Grammar/Format constraints guarantee STRUCTURE and TYPES, not SEMANTICS. The model can emit perfectly-valid JSON with an out-of-scope target, wrong CIDR, or destructive flag. Constrained decoding does NOT replace the Scope Guard — it sits before it. Always treat decoded actions as untrusted until both jsonschema-validated AND Scope-Guard-approved.

Native Ollama tool-call Arguments are parsed, not validated. Unlike the Format path, tools mode does not grammar-constrain argument generation, so you can get missing required fields or wrong types. You MUST validate ToolCalls arguments against the tool's schema before dispatch.

Deeply nested or recursive JSON Schemas hurt both reliability and latency under constrained decoding, and some schemas don't fully round-trip through json_schema->GBNF. Keep action schemas flat; split complex plans into multiple constrained calls.

Format and Tools interact awkwardly on some models/versions — forcing a Format while also offering Tools can suppress tool calls or vice-versa. Prefer a two-step design: one call to SELECT a tool (Tools), a second Format-constrained call to FILL that tool's args.

Model choice still matters: small/un-tool-trained models pick wrong tools or loop even with valid JSON. Smaller GPT-OSS variants specifically had broken structured-output enforcement with Ollama in late 2025 (Harmony format). Prefer Qwen3 14B/32B, Llama 3.1/3.3, or Devstral, and pin/version-test the model.

langchaingo as the core abstraction is a trap for this project: it lags the raw client, hides the request internals you need for auditing/control, and bloats the binary. Its WithTools/Ollama support works for prototyping but cedes determinism you want in a security tool. Use the raw api client.
Set temperature 0 (or very low) and a generous context (>=32k) for tool/structured calls; defaults cause avoidable format drift and dropped tool calls.
Fail closed, not open: if validate-and-repair exhausts retries, log an audited failure and abort the action — never execute a partially-parsed or 'best effort' action in a pen-test context.
Streaming + tool calls: if you stream (Ollama supports streaming tool calls since May 2025), accumulate and re-validate the full assembled tool call; don't act on partial fragments.
open_questions: Single fixed-schema-per-call (Format) vs. model-chooses-tool (Tools) vs. the recommended two-step hybrid — which fits strix's planner loop best? This depends on how the existing planner already frames plan steps.

Which exact local model(s) will strix pin as the default brain? That determines real-world tool-call accuracy and whether you can rely on native Tools mode or must fall back to Format-constrained single-tool calls.

Do you want to commit to Ollama as the only backend, or define a backend interface now (Ollama default, llama.cpp server as air-gapped/power-user) — the latter is cheap to design upfront but adds an abstraction.

Schema source of truth: generate JSON Schemas from Go structs (invopop / google/jsonschema-go) vs. hand-author GBNF for the tightest constraints on critical fields (tool name enum, risk category). A hybrid (auto schema + hand GBNF for the few safety-critical fields) may be ideal.
How many repair retries before fail-closed, and should repair attempts themselves be first-class audit-log entries (recommended yes for a pen-test tool)?
google/jsonschema-go (Jan 2026) vs. santhosh-tekuri for validation long-term — adopt the newer official package fully, or keep santhosh-tekuri for its broader draft/keyword coverage?
